titleStmt.title: To Harriet Shaw Weaver. Friday, 25 November 1921
titleStmt.author: James Joyce

seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p:
Dear Miss Weaver: I had an interview yesterday with the printer. From what I can gather a crisis seems to have been reached as a result of which I need £75 to pay him a draft falling due on the 30 November and to keep myself alive till the first week in December. I cannot find your letter (I cannot find anything now living as we do three in a room with my case of books stored and the table of my polar apartment, in which I sit wrapped in three shawls and blankets, piled with proofs), but it seems to me you said I could draw on some money – I forget what money it was but it must have been yours as usual. During the past few months I had to draw on the meagre sum set apart for the printer but it was said that a number of people were going to do a great many things which they haven’t done. Moreover, as far I can note there appears to have been a disagreement in the family of my publishers here (though I would ask you not to allude to this lest I should be promptly denounced as even more stupid than was thought) but there has certainly been one in the family of the translator of the passages for the lecture (card enclosed). Anyhow for the last two or three months the printer has shelved my book in favour of Mr Mac Almon McAlmon
’s (who, I take it, paid promptly and in advance). This latter is now out but for the past week not a single word has been set, the printers confining themselves to executing my corrections. This being the position I have no recourse but to write you this letter. I daresay you will think I am very mercenary. The printer told me that I have made such alterations on Ulysses as reduced my estimated gain (on total sale) by about £600 – and this after 7 ½ years labour. I cannot help it. I must give as much as I can. He says the book will weigh about 4 lbs. I suggest it be sold by the ounce. Typing has been a heavy item for me personally as I had certain parts done over three or four times to facilitate the printer in setting. Also I am afraid I must have the proofs of Ithaca (the ugly duckling of the book and therefore, I suppose, my favourite) read by a competent person – which will be another expense. I don’t believe there was ever a more tiresome person to all who have the misfortune to know him than I am. As for Ulysses it is a perfect nightmare to me. I could finish it off (in the murderer’s sense) in about 50 or 60 hours, I think, on proof – provided this engagement is met and the printers print the end of it rapidly.

The passages to be read at the séance are – the execution scene from the Cyclops, the romance in the Sirens, a few passages from Ithaca (which I insisted on), and the last six pages of the book from Penelope. I made out a rough chart of the book for Mr Larbaud in order to help him to confuse the audience a little more. I ought not to have done so and when he had seen it I asked him to send it back. Would you like to see it?
I hope when all is done you will give me a position as gardener though I shall spend as much time as possible sitting on the wheelbarrow.

div.note: A reading of passages from Ulysses translated into French, held on 7 December 1921 at La Maison des Amis des Livres, 7 rue de l’Odéon. JJ enclosed a handbill for the séance in his letter to Harriet Weaver of 6 December 1921.

The so-called “schema” of Ulysses, an outline of the themes associated with each episode, mentioned also in JJ’s letters to Larbaud of 6 November 1921 (LIII 53), 15 November 1921 (LIII 53), and 26 November 1921 (LIII 54).
